title: A guard shipped to the primitive is inert until the MCP server restarts, and nothing signals it
description:
Discovered 2026-08-04 while closing the ticket batch that added the guards, and confirmed by two independent observations. This is an operational hazard rather than a code bug, which is why nothing caught it.

**The shape.** `src/mcp-server.js` is bundled into `dist/mcp-server.cjs` and run as a long-lived stdio process. A guard added to `src/task-store.js` or `src/close-guard.js`, rebuilt into the bundle and committed, is **not executing** in any MCP server process that started before the rebuild. The code is correct, the bundle is fresh, `dist-parity` is green, every spec passes — and the running process is stale. Nothing anywhere signals the gap.

**Confirmed twice, empirically:**

1. **TASK-200 closed at 2026-08-04 09:58 with no pre-existing reviewer-authored comment**, 9.5 hours after TASK-187's evidence rule landed (`d97838b`, 00:29). Replaying `hasCommentFromAuthor` against its pre-close comment set returns `false`, so `checkCloseEvidence` would block that close today. It succeeded. (TASK-193 and TASK-189 also closed without one, but both predate the rule and are legitimate — TASK-200 is the decisive case.)
2. **TASK-201's sanitizer did not run** on a comment appended after `ffb1a53` rebuilt the bundle: three U+200D characters persisted into `tasks/TASK-201.json`. TASK-201's own AC6 corpus sensor correctly flagged them. The shipped bundle contains `sanitizeCommentBody`; the running server does not.

**Why it matters.** Every guard this session added at the primitive — TASK-186's UAT grammar, TASK-187's close preconditions, TASK-188's default-on loop guards and author enum, TASK-189's AC validation, TASK-201's sanitizer — is inert in the session that shipped it. Worse, the failure is silent and inverted: an operator sees green tests and a successful close and concludes the control works, when the control was simply absent. That is the same "looks active, is not" shape those tickets exist to eliminate, one layer down.

It also quietly invalidates a class of evidence. TASK-187's closing comment claimed its own close was "the feature's first live exercise" — corrected there — and any future ticket that verifies a guard by exercising it through the MCP tools during the same session it shipped will draw the same false conclusion.

**Not necessarily a code change.** The honest fix might be procedural (a documented restart step after any rebuild touching bundled guard code) or mechanical (a version/build stamp the server reports and something compares against the committed bundle). Decide deliberately. A mechanical signal is preferable because the procedural one has already failed once here.

**Do not over-engineer this.** Hot-reloading an MCP server is not in scope and would introduce more risk than it removes. The goal is that the discrepancy becomes *visible*, not that it becomes impossible.

**Note the scope boundary:** direct `src/` importers — the test suite, `bin/` CLIs, the wargame harness — always get the current code. Only the long-lived MCP server process is affected. Say so precisely in whatever gets documented, because overstating this would make people distrust green test runs that are genuinely trustworthy.
acceptance_criteria: The discrepancy between a running MCP server's loaded bundle and the committed dist/ bundle is detectable rather than silent. State plainly what the detection is and where it surfaces.

A decision is recorded on mechanical-vs-procedural: if a build stamp or version handshake is added, say what compares it and when; if the fix is documentation only, justify why a mechanical signal was rejected given the procedural approach already failed once.

The scope boundary is documented accurately: direct src/ importers (tests, bin/ CLIs, harnesses) always execute current code; only the long-lived MCP server process can be stale. Do not imply green test runs are untrustworthy.
The orchestrator-routing SKILL.md records what to do after a rebuild that touches bundled guard code, in both parity copies byte-identical.

A spec or sensor covers whatever mechanism is chosen, and fails if the mechanism is removed. If the fix is purely procedural and no sensor is possible, state that explicitly rather than shipping a decorative test.
npm run test:all is green; dist rebuilt and committed if bundled source changes, with dist-parity passing.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body:
**APPROVE** — final verdict across three rounds. FULL depth, tier `tests-after`. **0 HIGH / 0 MEDIUM outstanding (1 deferred by the Orchestrator) / all LOWs closed.**

Commits `2284100` (round 1) → `9fcc70e` (two-leg fix) → `8699a6d` (non-suppression lock, field rename, caveat completion). Non-contiguous — TASK-205/207/208 commits interleave.

**Gate, on a quiesced tree:** `test:all` **192 passed | 1 skipped (193 files), 2246 passed | 4 skipped, 0 failed**, 118.96s, exit 0 ⬛ `test:since -- 9fcc70e` 16 files / 276 passed, no zero-selection marker ⬛ ticket e2e 3 files / 46 passed ⬛ parity both SKILL.md copies `sha1 4bc5e54c028319a7f2e817f1e6696cfd20bae3c2` by direct hash ⬛ `check:calibration` clean.

Every failure the developer flagged resolved on its own and was attributed **empirically, not by assertion**: the `dist/pack-ctl.cjs` parity failure disappeared once TASK-207 committed and rebuilt (`dc4bc70`/`25255de`); `tests/mcp-tool-doc-lock.spec.js` is no longer untracked — it landed as TASK-208's `f490378`, runs 15 passed, and `mcp_build_status` now appears 5× in `tool-contract.md` in both parity copies. **TASK-208's sensor caught this ticket's own tool, and TASK-208 fixed it.**

## HIGH-1 (the plugin-cache false green) — closed, verified live

Round 2 rebuilt the real topology and ran it end-to-end through a spawned stdio process against the real repo: the drifted-cache case yields `self_stale: false` (the old single leg still says "fresh", exactly as it would have for TASK-200 and TASK-201) while `repo_divergent: true` fires. The Empty-result seam holds — a consumer project with no `dist/` yields `repo_reason: 'repo-bundle-missing'` and `repo_divergent: null`, **never `false`**. Leg independence verified in both directions, structurally (neither leg reads the other; the only shared gate is `!buildStamp`, which correctly disables both) and empirically.

## The non-suppression lock is guarded against going vacuous — this is the detail that matters

`tests/e2e/mcp-build-status.spec.js:157-160` asserts leg 1 is *genuinely* broken before asserting anything about leg 2:
```js
expect(result.self_checked).toBe(false);
expect(result.self_reason).toBe('bundle-missing');
expect(result.self_stale).toBeNull();
```
Without those three lines a future change that quietly stopped breaking leg 1 would leave `repo_checked: true` passing for the trivial reason — leg 2 works because leg 1 works — and the lock would go green while guarding nothing. With them, the test can only pass if leg 2 rendered a verdict **while leg 1 was down**, which is precisely the guarantee. The red-plant was confirmed by construction, not taken on faith: gating leg 2 behind `selfLeg.self_checked` trips exactly that assertion, and no other test in the file exercises a broken leg 1 alongside a live repo bundle, so one failure is the *correct* count rather than a suspiciously small one.

## The rename exclusion is right and complete

Every surviving bare `checked`/`reason` in `src/mcp-server.js` falls into three unrelated buckets: `verifyLinkedCommits`'s own return shape and JSDoc (its own distinct reason vocabulary — `'none-linked'`, `'git-unavailable'`, `'not-a-git-repo'`), the reference to it at :688, and `close_task`'s `exception: { reason }` schema — **a human-authored bypass justification that would have been actively wrong to rename.** Nothing belonging to `checkBundleFreshness` was missed; `dist/` carries the renamed fields and parity is green.

## The LOW-6 collapse lost nothing load-bearing

What moved to SKILL.md is rationale — the two incidents, the topology discovery, the counterfactual. What **stayed** at `src/mcp-server.js:65-90` is what a source reader cannot afford to go looking for: the two leg names, what each answers, and the full **scope-boundary paragraph verbatim**, including *"a green `npm test` / `npm run test:all` run is unaffected by this note and remains trustworthy evidence."* That is AC3's substance and the ticket's explicit warning against overstatement — had it been collapsed into the pointer this would have been a finding. ~70 lines → ~26, no contract lost.

The tool-description carve-out is not merely defensible, it is **the only correct answer**: an MCP tool description is the sole thing a client ever sees — another model, another session, a third-party client with no filesystem access. A SKILL.md pointer there would be inert text.

## Topology caveat — accurate; relay it, with one nuance

Every factual claim re-verified against machine state: `known_marketplaces.json` gives `hivemind-marketplace` as `{source: "git", url: "https://github.com/HexingBot/hivemind.git"}`; `installed_plugins.json` pins the install to the cache at 0.18.0, `gitCommitSha c3e7067`, updated 2026-07-27. A local `build:plugin` cannot reach it, a reconnect cannot reach it, `/plugin update` fetches only that remote. All three hold, and the new clause closes the exact trap — an operator following the old wording would have run `/plugin update`, gotten nothing, and had no idea why.

**Nuance, not a defect:** the clause states a *necessary* condition ("must be pushed... before"), which is strictly correct, but pushing is not quite *sufficient* — the marketplace pins a version (0.18.0 against a repo at 0.20.0), so a release/version bump is generally also needed before `/plugin update` picks it up.

**Verdict: APPROVE.** Three rounds, ending materially better than it started — not just fixed, but locked. Nothing from any round remains open except MEDIUM-3 (fold the freshness verdict into `close_task`'s envelope), deferred deliberately.

comments.author: orchestrator
comments.body:
**CLOSED on a green independent review after two fix rounds.** Review depth **FULL** throughout; rubric inputs: round 1 was 521 changed lines (507+/14-) across 7 files — over the 150 threshold — AND every round touches packaging/dist (`dist/mcp-server.cjs`), the MCP server surface, and shipped skill docs in two parity copies. Any one input forces FULL.

Commits `2284100` → `9fcc70e` → `8699a6d`, **non-contiguous** — TASK-205, TASK-207 and TASK-208 commits interleave. Tier `tests-after`, audited and confirmed defensible: the new tool is read-only, empty `inputSchema`, no state mutation or parsing.

## READ THIS FIRST — what closing this ticket does and does not mean

**The guards from TASK-186 through TASK-201 are still NOT executing in this session's MCP server.** This ticket makes that legible; it does not make it go away. Closing it must not be read as those guards now being live.

## The finding that reframed the whole problem

Round 1 built a sound mechanism watching the wrong file. The reviewer followed the path the developer's own startup log printed and found the real topology:

```
.mcp.json spawns ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/mcp-server.cjs
CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT -> ~/.claude/plugins/cache/hivemind-marketplace/hivemind/0.18.0
known_marketplaces.json -> source: git, url: https://github.com/HexingBot/hivemind.git   (REMOTE)
installed_plugins.json  -> version 0.18.0, gitCommitSha c3e7067, updated 2026-07-27

sha256 <cache>/dist/mcp-server.cjs = 51c377d3...   grep sanitizeCommentBody -> 0
sha256 <repo>/dist/mcp-server.cjs  = 2f9d0da9...   grep sanitizeCommentBody -> present
```

**The running server loads from the installed plugin cache, not this repo.** `npm run build:plugin` — the only rebuild anyone performs, and the one `dist-parity` guards — never touches that copy. So the round-1 check compared cache-then to cache-now and would have returned `stale: false` **for both incidents that motivated the ticket**, while its own description claimed it meant "this process matches the current committed bundle." That is the precise inversion the ticket exists to prevent: a control that looks active, is not, and now emits a green signal saying so.

This was not found by reading the diff. It was found by following a path into `~/.claude/plugins/` and hashing what was actually there — outside the repo entirely.

## The fix

`checkBundleFreshness` now reports **two independent legs**: `self_stale` (did the path I was spawned from mutate in place) and `repo_divergent` (do my loaded bytes differ from `<repoRoot>/dist/mcp-server.cjs`, the only file the build ever touches, **regardless of which path I was spawned from**). Each carries its own `checked`/`reason`. `repo-bundle-missing` — the normal consumer-project case — yields `repo_divergent: null`, **never `false`**, per the Empty-result contract. Verified live end-to-end through a real spawned stdio process against the real repo, in all three topologies.

## What the third round bought, and why it was worth one more pass

1. **The non-suppression lock, with a vacuity guard.** The design's central guarantee — neither leg suppresses the other — had no spec. The new lock asserts leg 1 is *genuinely* broken (`self_checked: false`, `self_reason: 'bundle-missing'`, `self_stale: null`) **before** asserting leg 2 still reports. Without those three lines the test would pass for the trivial reason once leg 1 stopped breaking, and would guard nothing. **This fix round existed precisely because a missing spec let the HIGH through**, so adding the lock rather than trusting the empirical proof was the right call.
2. **The field rename, done at the last moment it was free.** `checked`/`reason` → `self_checked`/`self_reason`, so a reader seeing `checked: false` cannot mistake it for "the whole check failed" — the exact state the reviewer's probe produced alongside a perfectly good `repo_divergent: true`. `mcp_build_status` was added **after v0.20.0 was cut and has never shipped**, so this cost nothing today and would have been a breaking change to a published tool contract next week. Timing was the entire argument.
3. **The topology caveat completed** — see below.

## The operator-facing payload (this is the ticket's real deliverable)

SKILL.md now states, in both parity copies, that closing `repo_divergent` needs a plugin update/reinstall rather than a reconnect — **and** that the work must already be reachable from the marketplace's remote, because an operator with unpushed local commits who runs `/plugin update` fetches only that remote and silently gets nothing.

**Nuance recorded for accuracy:** that clause states a *necessary* condition, correctly, but pushing is not quite *sufficient* — the marketplace pins a version (0.18.0 against a repo at 0.20.0), so a release/version bump is generally also needed before `/plugin update` picks the change up. The full operator sequence is therefore: **push → version bump/release → `/plugin update` → reconnect.**

## Cross-ticket note worth keeping

**TASK-208's sensor caught this ticket's own tool.** TASK-208 was split out of this review (rather than folded in, on the reviewer's argument that the durable fix is a mechanism deriving the documented tool list from `createServer`'s real registrations, not six hand edits). Its sensor then immediately flagged `mcp_build_status` as undocumented — a ticket written hours earlier catching a ticket written by a different agent. That is the split paying for itself on its first run.

## Findings status

HIGH-1 and HIGH-2 closed and verified live. LOW-5 (absolute claim about the load-to-`main()` window), LOW-6 (five-way duplication — collapsed to ~26 lines pointing at SKILL.md as canonical, while **keeping** the scope-boundary paragraph verbatim in source, since that was AC3's substance), the asymmetric naming, and the incomplete caveat are all closed. MEDIUM-4 closed elsewhere as TASK-208.

**MEDIUM-3 remains open by my deliberate deferral:** detection is on-demand only, so its *invocation* is still procedural — the same dependency the ticket says already failed once. The natural closure is folding the freshness verdict into `close_task`'s response envelope so the check rides the operation it protects. Not bolted on under time pressure; it deserves its own consideration.

AC3's scope boundary passed on first review and survived the collapse intact — it explicitly protects green test runs ("remains trustworthy evidence"), which is the harm the ticket warned against. Scope discipline held: no hot-reload, no auto-restart, no process management. The goal was visibility, and visibility is what shipped.
